titled "Rebuking Characteristics at Shaolin," "Niu Tou Distinguishes the Way," "Tong Tong, Shi Zi, Yuan De,
and the Red Pagoda of Xuedou," "Hanlin," "Fushan Lu Gong with His Long Beard and the Snow in the Incense Burner," and "Baoci’s Sword in the Void."
The Divine Cauldron shatters the cake; Zhaozhou cuts the firewood. Shichuang visits his mother;
Dongshan bids farewell to his kin. Shishuang and Leiqian; Miaoxi’s seasonal freshness. Jianyuan seeks the bone; Yun’an displays the true [face].
Chijue blurs the eyes; Huijiao locks the mouth. Shandeng’s hundred clumsy acts; Daoyuan’s five pecks.
Shiqu mistook a frog; Yingzhen struck a dog. Lianfeng’s staff, Songyuan’s broom—Congyue’s lychees, Chuning’s radish, Zhenxie’s changing of robes. Qian’an declined his robe;
Zuqing’s twenty chopsticks. Jie’an’s single bowl of porridge, Tanhua’s tender peach—Fachang’s ripened plum.
Daoxin did not use a rope; Huineng lacked a sieve. Linji struck his father;
Huangbo surpassed his master. Taling had a pearl; Xiangyan had no awl. Huiri discussed medicine; Chaishi was because of chess.
Zuyuan disciplined the spirit; Tianran rode upon the sage. Da sui provided service; Yin zhi maintained purity.
Yuanzhao brought it back; Hongzhi carried it forth. Jizhao followed the record; Huazhi guarded the command.
Ciming occasionally desired it; Baiyun was too early. This-Arn and Budai; Xuefeng’s colander.
Hui’an’s winnowing basket; Cijue encouraged inquiry. Daowu delighted in the Way.
Baizhang’s Zen dwelling; Dajue’s Menglou Hall; De’ung’s large bowls; Zibo’s ginger;
Niutou’s pickled vegetables; Fuyong’s rice soup; or the hermitage with its child; Mingjiao’s “this lad”;
Huoshan’s four vines; Lepu’s single arrow; Duan’s establishment of the Patriarchs’ Hall; and Jian’s dismantling of the Buddha Hall.
Yuedang declined the invitation; Yuyuan prepared several courses of food. Yunding [harmonized] the Three Teachings; Faquan [possessed] ten thousand scrolls. Ehu’s lake and moon;
Nanyue’s Tianze and Baozhang lived for a thousand years. Zhaozhou [lived] seven hundred years; Yihuai set down his carrying pole.
Zihui personally labored at the stone wall; Yi’an shared the toil. Zhenru personally performed the service.
Letang’s mercury and quicksilver; Yunmen’s cinnabar; Huangbo has not much to say; Guizong’s calculations are slight;
Fayan is not yet finished; Dajue is too far off. Ye County returns the flour; Yuan Tong convenes for tea;
Yangshan’s circular marks; Yantou’s letter "I"; Gaoan laments its extravagance; Hongzhi assists with the deficiency.
Shitou’s grass hut; Bajiao’s mulberry-bark robe; Shanxian’s ingratitude; Qinlao’s change of lineage to Deshan;
Jieti’s iron [clout]; Huanyong’s bell-sound; Jingyin’s sweeping the bamboo; Qinglin’s planting pines;
Zhenji’s dismantling his residence; Foguo’s extinguishing of the school; Wuzhu’s court crows; Shenzan’s window bees.
Qianfeng’s Dharmakāya; Jianfu’s own self; Ying’an’s vipers and snakes; Furi’s insects and vermin;
Ken’an’s baskets and chests; Xiuyong’s luggage; Huiyuan’s single exchange; Jingshen’s great death; Jicui’s selling of treasures;
Yangqi’s polishing of gems; Foyan’s inscriptions on the wall; Huichang’s signboards over the gates.
Sishin’s first-place ranking; Huian’s status as a *zhuangyuan*; Shaolin’s blossoming of the flower; Caoxi’s returning to the root;
Fayen’s six aspects; Ciming’s three seals; "withered meditation" (*kuchan*) and the falling of the mirror; Ruiguang’s drum thundering; Wujian’s returning of the bond;
Xueque’s returning of the gift; Zhekuai’s declining the courtesy; and Zhibing’s casting away of the letter of credit.
Huayan’s coiled dragon; Touzi’s soaring falcon; Yongan’s steady vision; Huiji’s dream ascent;
Huizhao’s pearl-bright clarity; Yezhu’s river-increasing; Yu Xian’s striking the tile;
Zaoxian’s knocking on ice; Fuxin’s advancing song; Fenyang’s initial verse; Guizong’s true medicine; Meng’an’s poisonous seed.
*De cuo jiangjun yuanyue sengtong fayun shidi: Dayi niansong chanyuan mengqiu shiyi*, Scroll One,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi [Name Missing].
The Shaolin Rejection of Characteristics; Niu-tou’s Discernment of the Penetrating.
The *Biyan Lu* states: "Bodhidharma observed from afar that this land possessed the karmic capacity for the Mahāyāna.

He consequently crossed the sea specifically to arrive here, transmitting the mind-seal alone to reveal the path to those lost in delusion. He did not establish written words, but directly pointed to the human mind so that one might see one's own nature."
He attained Buddhahood. When he first met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor did not accord with his realization; consequently, he secretly crossed the Yangtze River to the Wei kingdom.

He went directly to Shaolin Temple, where he sat facing a wall for nine years and received the Second Patriarch. At that time, the Wei Dynasty’s Vinaya Master Guangtong and the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci debated with the Master;
the Master rebuked their attachment to forms and pointed toward the Mind, but they were both unable to bear his breadth of perspective and rose up in competition against him.

The malicious ones repeatedly added poison to his food; by the sixth time, his work of transformation was complete, he had found those to whom he could transmit the Dharma, and thus he no longer sought to save them.

He passed away while sitting upright and was buried at Dinglin Temple on Mount Xiong’er. Later, during the Later Wei dynasty, Song Yun, while serving as an envoy to the Pamir Mountains, encountered the Master traveling there carrying a single shoe in his hand.
The *Chuan deng lu* states: "The Chan Master Fayong of Mount Niutou in Jinling was nineteen years old when his studies of the classics and histories were complete.

He subsequently read the great Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and attained a profound understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*). He suddenly sighed, saying: 'The secular texts of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma;

the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. Thereupon, he went into seclusion at Maoshan to receive a teacher and tonsured his head. Later, he entered Mount Niutou..."
In a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Tou, there was a marvel of various birds carrying flowers in their beaks. The *Zongjing Lu* states:

"The Prince of Pengcheng asked the various venerable masters: 'If you have realized the fruits and attained the state of a sage, then let water flow from my left armpit and fire emerge from my right armpit;
let us fly through the void, emit light, and cause the earth to tremble. Then I shall pay homage to you.'"
When asked about his teacher, Niutou Rong Daoshi replied: "If one were to demand of me such a realization of the fruit [of enlightenment] as you do now, I fear it would deviate from the Way.

If becoming a Buddha were truly like this, then even a master of illusions could become a Buddha. In the past, when Śākyamuni expounded the Unsurpassed Way amidst the Sangha, he was no different from the monks;
when Vimalakīrti spoke of the fruit of liberation while among the laity, he was no different from the laypeople."
In the case of the woman Śrīmālā, she preached the Mahāyāna Dharma while her female form remained unchanged.

In the case of the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, he practiced the conduct of an icchantika while his monastic appearance did not shift. This is based precisely on the distinction between whether their inner minds understand or do not understand.
What has this to do with the physical body, male or female appearance, or the beauty or ugliness of one’s clothing?

If it were said that a sage is one whose form changes according to their realization and whose features shift following their awakening, then only when Gautama’s form changed would he become Śākyamuni, and only when Vimalakīrti’s appearance shifted would he become Kanakamuni.
Thus we know that realization is a realization of the mind and not a transformation of the form; awakening is a transformation of wisdom and has no concern with the difference of appearances.

For example, when an official in the world is promoted or transferred, does his appearance change simply because his rank has become higher? *Dàotōng shízǐ* (The Purple Stone of Dàotōng) states: "Dàotōng Chánshī of Zǐyù Mountain in Tángzhōu.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, Mázǔ... [The text continues: "...expounded [the Dharma].

*Chuándēng lù* (The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) states: "Dàotōng Chánshī of Zǐyù Mountain in Tángzhōu. During the early Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, Mázǔ... [The text continues: "...established [his teaching]."

He converted Jianyang and resided at Foji Rock. The Master went there to visit him. Later, when Mazu was about to pass away, he said to the Master, "The jade and stone are moist and the mountains are lush and beautiful;
these will further your dharma practice. When you encounter such a place, you may dwell there. The Master did not understand his words.
That autumn, he traveled to Luoyang together with Master Zizai of Mount Founiu.

Upon returning and reaching the west of Tangzhou, he saw a mountain whose four sides were precipitous and whose peaks were exceptionally beautiful. He inquired of the local people, who told him it was Mount Ziyu.
The Master then climbed to the summit of the mountain and saw a stone that was square, brilliant, and purple in color. He sighed and said, "This must be that 'Purple Jade'."
He first reflected that the words of his former teacher were indeed a prophecy. He then cut reeds to construct a hut and dwelt therein.
Later, disciples gathered from the four quarters.
The *Sengbao zhengxu zhuan* states: "The Chan Master’s name was Daomin. When he reached the capital of Daliang for official studies, he suddenly grew weary of worldly dust and secular life."
He received full ordination and traveled extensively to consult with masters of the lineage. He stayed the longest under Master Zhenru Zhe.

Later, hearing of the spiritual reputation of Chan Master Ledu Qian of Lantian, he went to rely upon him. Upon their first meeting, Qian recognized that he was the one whom the assembly at Daopei called the "Ancient Buddha Min."
He [Yunmen] held him in deep esteem. On another day, he said to him, "Mount Lu is magnificent and peerless; your karmic conditions are ripe there.
He then took his leave and went forth into the world at Guankxi in Jiangxia, later moving to Yuantong on Mount Lu. Initially, Chan Master Daoyi had founded and reformed Yuantong.
At the time of his death, he left this instruction: "My stupa shall be made of green stone. If the stupa turns red on another day, it means I have returned.
On the very evening the Master arrived, the stupa turned red. People from near and far were struck with wonder and realized that the Master was indeed the reincarnation of Daoji.

Consequently, the school’s tradition flourished to the height of its glory, and monks flocked there like clouds. The details regarding the posthumous title of Master Yuande, who provided spiritual succor, and the matter of the inscription on his stupa, are recorded in the *Sengbao zhuan*.
The *Sengbaozhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) by Fushan Lu of Xuedou Hanlin states:
The Chan Master’s name was Chongxian, his style name was Yinzhi. From childhood he was sharp and vigorous; in his studies he grasped the essentials, and his penmanship was swift and nimble.
In his prime, he excelled at calligraphy and composed verses of Dharma (*dharmapada*), emulating the Chan Master Xiu of Cien Monastery. He once traveled...
At Xixian on Mount Lu, Chan Master Shi resided. He was austere and rarely received visitors;

because he appeared coarse and unrefined, Xian did not harmonize with him and composed a poem on Lion Peak (the peak is located at Xixian) to satirize him: "His posture crouching on the ground, his power never ceasing;

How could his claws and fangs ever mingle with the common herd? Heaven ordained his birth upon a thousand peaks; Even without clouds supporting him, he still sticks out his head. Later, [Xian] resided at...
At Xuedou in Mingzhou, the patriarchal style flourished greatly; monks from all over the land—like dragons coiled and phoenixes soaring—vied to gather at his seat.
The *Biyánlu* states: "Some have discussed this, praising Xuedou for possessing the talent of a Hanlin scholar."
The *Sengbao zhuan* states: The Chan Master’s name was Fayuan. Initially, he accepted an invitation to Taiping Monastery in Shuzhou and later resided at Fushan for a short time.
He traveled through Sichuan with seven companions, including Daguang Ying and Xue Datou; they nearly encountered a violent disaster, but Yuan delivered them from it through his wisdom.
Because the group recognized his proficiency in administrative affairs, they called him "Master Yuan Lu" (the Registrar).
*Chángzī Lúxuě* (Long-Bearded Snow on the Incense Burner).
From the *Jùtóng Jì* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp): When Chan Master Chángzī Kuàng of Tánzhōu first went to Cáoxī to pay respects at the Patriarch’s stupa, he returned to visit Shítóu.
Shítóu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lǐngnán. Shítóu said, "On the summit of the ridge is a single honored one..."
"Have you achieved the perfection of merit? The Master said, "I have achieved it long ago; I simply lack the 'dotting of the eyes' (the final realization).
Shitou asked, "Do you wish for me to dot your eyes? The Master replied, "Please do so. Shitou then lifted one foot. The Master prostrated himself.
Shitou asked, "What principle did you perceive that you prostrate yourself? The Master replied, "According to what I have seen, it is like a great furnace."
A touch of snow above.
The *Chuan deng lu* records that Master Panshan Baoji addressed the assembly, saying: "The moon of the mind is solitary and full; its light swallows the myriad phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist. When both light and objects have vanished, what is it then? O Zen adepts, it is like this:"
It is like casting a sword into the void; one need not deliberate whether it reaches its mark or not. This is because the empty wheel leaves no trace and the blade suffers no loss.

If you can be thus, then mind after mind is without cognition. The whole mind is the Buddha, and the whole Buddha is the person. When person and Buddha are without distinction, only then does one become the Way.
The Divine Cauldron Shatters the Biscuit; Zhaozhou Cuts the Firewood.
The *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) states: Chan Master Hongyin was in seclusion at Sengsheng Zang on Mount Heng.

A man from Xiangyin named Bangcheng, of a prominent clan, came to visit Fuyan and entered the chamber of Hongyin. There he beheld Hongyin’s appearance—serene and tranquil—holding but a single alms bowl.

[He] hung [the image] on the wall; no one could distinguish between intimacy and distance. [The donor] became so deeply attached that he forgot to leave. He said, "Master, would you rather remain a long-term guest to others, or would you wish to dwell in the mountains?
My home is beneath Shending; it is a neighboring temple and the place where my family has planted merit for generations, yet it has long lacked a presiding abbot.
You may go there together. Yìn laughed and said, "Yes. Thereupon, he loaded Yìn onto his own horse and returned him [to the mountain]. Yìn...
He arrived. They provided fish, drums, congee, and rice as is customary in various regions. Within one year, the monastic community was established;
after ten years, there were thirty monks. When the monk Qi Sōng visited while still young, Yìn sat in the hall receiving his formal prostration.
Pointing to two small jars in the courtyard, he said, "The time for your arrival has finally come. This year, the temple will finally have sauce for its meals. The next day—

Holding a basket with both hands, he took the food and threw it into the monks' alms bowls. Hui-sōng surveyed them from top to bottom; some were chewing immediately, while others left the food as it was.
Hui-sōng tucked it into his sleeve and went down from the hall to observe that they were all broken cakes and biscuits.
He questioned the elders, who said, "This temple has never cooked porridge since its founding. If there is a donor requesting a meal offering, Master Hui-yin serves it in order."
He dispatched a monk to go there. The master instructed him to take the dry, leftover portions back and store them beneath the granary;
he was to crush and roast them, then divide them equally to serve as flour. The Abbot said, "It is truly fitting that you arrived just at this moment.
Daosong was greatly astonished. There was a wooden bench; one night, Huian sat upon it, while about thirty people surrounded him to listen to his instructions.
The *Biographical Account of Chan Master Zhaozhou Zhenji* states: The Master’s name was Congshen. Carrying his water jar and staff, he traveled extensively throughout all quarters.
He often said of himself: "If a seven-year-old child surpasses me, I shall question him; if a hundred-year-old elder falls short of me, I shall instruct him.
When he reached the age of eighty, he finally resided at Guanyin Temple to the east of Zhaozhou City.
The abbot of the monastery was austere in character and emulated the ancients. The monks' hall lacked front and rear galleries; he would prepare meals on the spot.
When a rope bed had a leg break, he would burn it for fuel, using only broken wood tied together with rope. Whenever others attempted to construct something new, the Master did not permit it.
Having served as abbot for some forty years, he never once sent a single letter to inform his patrons.
Shichō Sōbo (Stone Window Visits His Mother):
Regarding Dongshan’s Parting from His Parents, the *Rentian Baoguan* states: Zen Master Shichō Kō long relied upon Zen Master Hongzhi of Tiantong.
He underwent trials in every duty, both great and small. One day, he returned to visit his mother. His mother said, "The purpose of your journey was originally to realize birth."

"You have died and delivered us, your parents, from suffering, and you shall long serve as a ruler of men. If you do not clearly understand cause and effect, it will bring trouble upon me in the underworld.
Gong replied, "In my dealings with the Sangha, I have not deceived them by even a hair’s breadth; even a single lamp-flame was used according to its proper purpose.
There is no need to worry about me. His mother said, "That may be so, but can one cross water without getting one's feet wet?"

Regarding the verses of the various patriarchs, Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie’s letter to his parents states: "I have humbly heard that when the Buddhas appear in the world, they all receive their bodies from their parents;
when the myriad species arise and flourish, they all depend on heaven and earth for their shelter and support.
Thus, there is no birth without parents, and no growth without heaven and earth. All beings are moistened by the grace of nurturing, and all receive the protection of their covering."
This is recorded in the *De* (Virtue). Alas! All sentient beings and the myriad forms of phenomena belong to impermanence; none have escaped birth and death.

Although the affection shown through nursing is profound and the kindness of raising one is deep, even if one were to provide worldly offerings and sustenance, it would ultimately be impossible to repay them.
How could service that consists of feeding on blood last forever? Thus, the *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "Though one uses the three sacrificial animals daily..."

To fail to provide for them is itself unfiliality. Thus, we are mutually entangled and submerged, forever entering the cycle of saṃsāra. There is no way to repay the boundless, profound kindness of one's parents better than through the merit of leaving the household life.

By cutting across the river of craving that binds birth and death and crossing the bitter sea of afflictions, one repays the parents of a thousand lifetimes and answers the grace of compassionate kin over ten thousand kalpas;
there is no fourfold debt within the three realms of existence that will not be repaid. Therefore, a sutra says:
"When one son leaves the household to become a monk, the nine generations of his clan are born in heaven. I, Liang-jia, renounce my body and life in this world, vowing never to return home.
I shall take these eternal roots and sense-fields to suddenly clarify Prajñā. I humbly entreat you, Father and Mother, to open your hearts with joyful relinquishment;
let your minds not cling to external conditions. Model yourselves after King Śuddhodana and emulate the noble Queen Māyā. In time to come, we shall meet at the Buddha’s assembly."
We have met; yet on this very day and at this very hour, we must part. It is truly not that I wish to hastily abandon your sweet and wholesome care, but rather that time does not wait for man.
Thus it is said: "If this body is not delivered in this life, when else shall it be delivered? I humbly hope that you will not harbor thoughts of longing for me. A verse says:
"Before realizing the source of the mind, many springs have passed; I sigh in vain at how one idly wanders through this floating world."
How many have attained the Way within the gate of emptiness? I alone remain lingering in the dust of the world. I respectfully prepare this brief letter to bid farewell to my loved ones;

I vow to clarify the Great Dharma as my repayment for my compassionate parents. There is no need to shed tears or remember me often; it is as if I had never existed from the very beginning. It is further said:
"The white clouds beneath the crags are my constant companions; the green barriers before the peaks serve as my neighbors. Thus one is spared from worldly entanglements.
Worldly fame and profit shall forever part from human love and hate. The Patriarchal intent is to be understood directly beneath a word;

the profound mystery must be penetrated within the truth of a phrase. Should you wish to meet your kinsmen of the entire clan, you must simply await the causal conditions for realizing the fruit in the future.
Shishuang Lei Qian. *Dahui Shixian Shitian Lu* states:
Chan Master Qingzhu, the successor of Daowu (whose name was Zongzhi), resided at Shishuang, which was one hundred and twenty li away.
Every new and full moon, he would invariably walk there to pay homage at the stupa of Daowu; even in his old age, he did not cease this practice. One night, a thunderbolt struck...
It rained. The pagoda shifted of its own accord to accommodate it; to this day, it is called the "Pagoda Relocated by Thunder" (Leiqian Ta).
The *Dahui Wuku* states: Every year when the Master (Dahui) obtained seasonal delicacies, he would first offer them to the Buddha and to Yuanwu before daring to taste them himself.
He said to his attendants, "Were it not for the Buddha and the Old Monk, how could I obtain such things?"
*Jianyuan Miji* (The Bone-Seeking of Jianyuan).

The *Zhengfayan Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) states: One day, Chan Master Jianyuan Zhongxing (who was a dharma heir of Daowu), while holding a spade in the Dharma Hall, walked from east to west and from west to east.
Shishuang asked, "What are you doing? The Master replied, "I am seeking the remains of my late teacher."
“Bones,” said Shishuang. “The vast waves are surging and the white billows reach to heaven; what spiritual bones are you looking for?
The Master replied, “This is precisely where one must exert effort. Shishuang said, “In this place, not even a needle can pierce it; what effort could there be?”
Wuku said: "Once, Zen Master Zhenjing suddenly called to his attendant, 'Bring the portrait of the Old Monk.
When the attendant spread out the portrait of National Teacher Nan, Zhenjing placed his hands over his forehead and said, 'Were it not for this old monk, how could such a thing be?
He then frowned for a long while before finally commanding that it be put away. He did this repeatedly."
*Chijue Yi Jing*: "Wisdom-Enlightenment Locks the Mouth.
*Kuya Manlu* states: The Chan Master Chijue Chong said, "In the past, while at Guifeng for three years, Cao Yuan’s anger, abuse, laughter, and jesting were all skillful means for the sake of others.
From that point on, I had no further doubts regarding the elder masters who arrived."
"You cannot deceive me. Thereafter, he lived freely and expansively according to conditions. Twenty years after Caoyuan Shunji passed into stillness, he was brought forth for the sake of others.
I dare not forget offering this incense; indeed, there are those among the brothers gathered from six locations who cannot be said to be lacking.
It is simply that those who employ the "obscuring the eyes" method (*yi-jing fa*) are few. How bitter! Our school is being lost.
The *Chuan Deng Lu* states: Regarding Chan Master Guangyun Huijue, a monk asked, "I have heard that Huijue possesses the 'seal-of-the-mouth' instruction (*suo-kou jue*)."
"How do you show this to people? The Master said, "It depends on my staff not being in my hand. The monk said, "If that is so, I deeply appreciate your kindness.
The Master said, "Wait until I grant you my approval, then you will have it."
Regarding "The Hundred Clumsinesses of Sōtō":
In the fifth year of Dōgen (1253), Kūya’s *Manroku* states: "Zen Master Hōon Sōtō was by nature utterly devoid of artifice; his witty sayings were all plain and straightforward.
Thus, he received the title 'The Hundred Clumsinesses.'"
Wuku said: "Baofeng Yuan was a man of the Way whose capacity for responding to the sharp point of a kōan was dull.
Juefan called him 'Yuan Wudou' (Yuan the Five-Dou), because he would have to open his mouth to draw in breath and cook five dou of rice before he could utter a single turning word.
'Yuan' is sometimes written as 'Yuan'."
Shiqi Listens to Frogs. *Yingzhen Zhuanggou Luhuyulu* states:
When the Head Seat Shiqi was first in meditative seclusion at Longmen in Shuzhou, he suddenly heard a chorus of frogs while dozing.
Mistaking them for the sound of a shaving board, he hurried toward them. Someone enlightened him, saying, "Those are frogs."
Qichu struck the sounding board. Startled and bewildered, he went to the abbot’s quarters to reveal his realization. Foyan said, "Have you not heard of Rāhula?
Qichu immediately stopped him, saying, "Master, there is no need to cite that; I will go and see for myself. Not long after, he attained enlightenment and composed this verse:
"Hearing the sound of the sounding board in a dream, Upon waking, the toad croaks. The toad and the sound of the sounding board— At once, the mountains and peaks [resound]."
He practiced with such diligence that he increasingly deepened his investigation and attained profound mastery of the subtle mysteries.
*Rendian baodian* states: "Under the guidance of Chan Master Deshan Muzhi, there was a practitioner who applied himself with exceptional vigor."
The Chan practitioner had long been unable to penetrate the koan regarding the dog having no Buddha-nature.
One day, he suddenly saw a dog’s head as large as the sun’s orb, opening its mouth as if to devour him. Terrified, the practitioner rose from his seat and fled.

When a neighbor asked him the reason, the practitioner explained the incident in detail and subsequently reported it to Deshan. Deshan said, “There is no need for fear. Simply exert your utmost vigor and wait for it.”
He opened his mouth. The meditator entered within and was finished. Following these instructions, the meditator sat until midnight when the dog appeared as before.
The meditator struck it with his head with all his might, and it was then inside a chest. Thereupon, he attained sudden and profound enlightenment.
Later, he appeared in the world at Wenshu, where his Way and Dharma flourished greatly; he was none other than Master Zhen.
The Lotus Peak Cudgel and the Songyuan Broom. The *Biyán Lù* states:
The Hermit of Lotus Peak held up his staff and addressed the assembly, saying, "When the ancients arrived here, why did they refuse to stay?
The assembly was speechless. He provided this substitute answer on their behalf: "Because they could not gain strength on the journey. Furthermore...

He asked, "Ultimately, how is it? He then spoke on his own behalf, saying: "Carrying my staff slung across my shoulder, heedless of others, I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks."
Chan Master Songyuan Yue’s verse for sending off a fundraising monk says: "A broom-handle worn out over many years, Casually picked up, it settles the fundamental纲 (guidelines) of the school.
This particular character is naturally unique; It is not like the "Old Eight" fellows found elsewhere.
The old saying that the Chan community transmits the "Songyuan Broom" phrase originated from this very verse.
Regarding Yue Lizhi: As for Ning Lubu, the *Wuku* (Armory Record) states:
"The Senior Seat-holder Qing Su was a native of Min. He attended Ciming for thirteen years. At the age of eighty, he resided at Luyuan in Huxiang;
he never initiated social interaction with others, and no one knew him. By chance, there was the Senior Seat-holder Yue, a native of Chuzhou."

He lived as a neighbor to Foyue. One day, while eating lychees preserved in honey, Fosu happened to pass by his door. Foyue called out to him, saying, "These are the local fruits of this old man's village; you may share them.
Fosu replied, "It has been a long time since I have had the opportunity to eat these since my former teacher passed away.
Foyue asked, "Who was your former teacher? Fosu said, "Ciming. Foyue was then struck with doubt and wonder, and he subsequently offered him the remaining fruit.
Gradually, he grew close to him. Later, Xu asked, "Who was it you saw? Yue replied, "The Venerable Wén of Dòngshān.

Xu asked again, "And who did Wén see? Yue replied, "Nán the Head Monk. Xu said, "It has not been long since Nán the Junior Monk saw our late master, yet his Dharma path has already flourished in such a way.

"The mind is Buddha; I dwell right here. A monk said, "Master Ma’s teaching of the Dharma has recently changed.

The monk returned and reported this to Mazu. Mazu said, "The assembly, the plum has ripened. From then on, students gradually flocked to him, and his reputation as a teacher grew ever more prominent.

"The Great Master Sengcan had a śrāmaṇera named Dōshin, who was fourteen years of age. He paid obeisance to the Master, saying:

The Master said, "Why seek further liberation? At these words, Xinxing attained great enlightenment. The *Zuting shiyuan* states:

(Eventually) the Patriarch secretly went to the rice-pounding shed and saw Huineng with a stone belt around his waist pounding rice.

He reached the point where he should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. Upon these words, he attained great enlightenment. The Patriarch, knowing that he had realized his original nature, transmitted the Sudden Teaching along with the robe and bowl, saying:

Those who have realized the Way in all quarters All say this is the highest level of capacity. When Guishan heard this, he said, "This child has attained thorough penetration. At that time, Yangshan said, "This..."
"This mind-mechanism of consciousness has produced this composition; it must wait for Huiji to personally examine it before it can be finalized.

The Master also composed a verse, saying: "Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty; this year’s poverty is truly poverty.
Last year’s poverty still allowed for the space to set up a single awl; this year’s poverty, there is not even an awl. Yangshou said:
"You may have understood the Buddha-dhyāna, Master, but you have not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna. The Master again composed a verse, saying: "I have a device; in a single blink—"

*Huirì Lùnyào* (Medicines from the Sun of Wisdom). *Cháishí Yīnqílúhú Yělù* states:
Chan Master Huìrì Yǎ of Mount Lú was a preeminent disciple of Zhēnjìng. He once composed an essay titled "Chan Bǎocǎo" (The Materia Medica of Chan), which says:
"The flavor of Chan is sweet and its nature is cool; it calms the heart-organ, dispels pathogenic qi, clears obstructions, and promotes circulation."
It clears the blood vessels, purifies the spirit, and benefits the will; it preserves the complexion, removes feverish affliction, and eliminates filth and evil.
It effectively neutralizes all poisons and can regulate myriad ailments. Among the medicinal plants found among humans, there are differences of size, skin, flesh, marrow, essence, and coarseness;
those that obtain the essence are considered superior. Therefore, they can heal both ordinary and holy beings, regardless of their rank. Others mostly grow in thickets and forests.
In chanting the wind and singing to the moon, there are many in this world who gather mere sounds and husks as medicine; those who consume them bring ruin to human life and nature.
Whether hidden or manifest, none but a realized one can recognize it. Without relying on cultivation or processing, a single dose liberates one from suffering, like the release of bonds;
its efficacy is divine, bestowing longevity upon people. Therefore, the Buddhas and Patriarchs used this medicine for healing.
He is the great King of Physicians for all the ailments of sentient beings; he is the bright lamp of the world that shatters the darkness of all attachments. Alas, how tragic!

Those whose minds are deluded and confused, who are shrouded in obscurity and lack faith, whose illnesses have reached the depths of the gallbladder and diaphragm, and who are defiled by false demons as they drift through the cycle of birth and death—these cannot be saved. How lamentable! Oh!
The *Sengbao zhuan* states: When Master Fushan Yuan first encountered him, Ou-yang Wen-chung Gong heard that Yuan was extraordinary and refined, so he visited his quarters;

yet, Yuan did nothing to distinguish himself. While playing chess with a guest, Yuan sat beside them. When Wen-chung finished the game, he requested Yuan to expound the Dharma by means of the chessboard.
Yuan then struck the drum, ascended the seat, and said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like two players setting their pieces against one another."

It resembles [the true thing], but what does this mean? When facing an opponent who understands the music, one must not yield in the moment of action. Only when one can string together five notes and add three more, and furthermore penetrate a single path, will it be attained.
There is a certain class of people who only know how to make a living by closing the door; they do not understand how to seize the corner and charge through the pass.
The hard nodes and the tiger’s mouth are both clearly manifest; once the position is broken, all efforts at maneuvering are in vain. Thus it is said:

"It is easy to gain fat on the edges, but difficult to find leanness in the belly. If one thinks before acting, one often loses the connection; if the mind is coarse, one frequently strikes one's head.

Do not boast of being a national master; do not vainly speak of being an immortal. Whether winning the game or losing the pieces is of no concern—tell me, when black and white have not yet been distinguished, what is there to say?
At that moment, where did the one who was struck down land? After a long silence, he said: "From the nineteen paths of old, how many have been deluded and how many have attained awakening?
Wen Zhong sighed deeply for a long time.
Regarding the Precepts of Zen Master Zuoyuan:

Later, he resided at Fuyan Hermitage in Lianjiang County. His community was so large and his duties so numerous that he had no leisure even by day.

He entered the hall and looked at him, saying, "My son is Tianran (Natural). The Master immediately descended from his seat, prostrated, and said, "I thank you for bestowing this Dharma name.

And yet you say, "I understand the supramundane Dharma. You do not even understand mundane dharmas!

Lao Yiqin. The Elder once instructed him that his fortune was meager and that he should not enter the world to become a human being;

Their views are biased and narrow, and their practice is indolent and lax. Some loftily extol the sacred realms while neglecting their own spiritual nature;

This is the sin of indolence. Why not once again leave the house of affliction and sever anew the net of worldly toil?
Drinking in the pure breeze, one seeks out the stream of the Way; probing subtle words, one searches for a kindred spirit.

With staff and *śikya* in hand, one performs walking meditation by green mountains and clear waters.

Suddenly, as if the light of the mind has broken through, doubts and obstructions melt away like ice. With clarity attained directly beneath, how could one remain ignorant of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?
The ultimate fruit is inherently complete; what hindrance could there be to the causal blossoms of the myriad practices?

Thus, both the essence and the teachings are mastered together, like the bright sun beautifying the realm of empty space; body and mind are both tranquil, like lapis lazuli containing the light of the precious moon.

He did not establish a Buddha hall, but erected only a Dharma Hall (*dharmasabhā*) to signify that the Buddhas and Patriarchs had personally transmitted their entrustment to him for his own generation.
This was done out of respect for their dignity. The assembled students of the school, regardless of their number or status, were all admitted into the Sangha Hall.
There, they were arranged according to the sequence of their seniority (*kṣayānupūrvī*), and ten administrative duties were established, known as the "Liaoshe" (administrative offices).

Each office employed a head official to supervise many subordinates, ensuring that all affairs were managed according to their respective jurisdictions. This unique practice of the Chan school originated with Baizhang.

From this, the Master’s reputation and virtue spread even further throughout the world.

The *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) states: When Chan Master Huoshan Jingtong first visited Yangshan, Yangshan sat with his eyes closed.
The Master said, "It is thus, it is thus. The twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven were also thus; the Sixth Patriarch of China was also thus."
"It is so. It was thus with my Upādhyāya; it was thus with Jingtong. Having finished speaking, he stood on his right leg with one foot raised.

Yangshan rose and struck him four times with a rattan staff. From this, the Master called himself "The Great Zen Buddha under Mount Jiyun who received four blows of the rattan staff from Heaven. Later, he resided at Huoshan.
The *Chuan Deng Lu* states: Chan Master Yuan’an of Lebu Mountain first sought the Way from Cuiwei Linji.
Linji frequently praised him before the assembly, saying: "A single arrow from Linji’s gate—dare anyone face its point?"
The Preface to the Ancestral Hall Regulations by Chan Master Baiyun Yuan states: "Our Way flourishes here in this land;
it is the legacy of the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, that established its fundamental principles. It is the system of Baizhang Dazhi that instituted the regulations for the Zen forest. This...
This is truly something known by all under heaven. Yet, how is it that within the ancestral halls of the world, each takes the founder of their own lineage as its patriarch?
They fail to consider whether this is what was most fundamentally transmitted and upheld by their own sect and ancestors. Alas!
Five hundred years after the arrival of the Teaching, Bodhidharma first came; would the worthies of the various schools of the past not have [recognized this]?
To know that one’s nature is itself the Sage—why then persist in being mired by the very notions of "nature" and "sage"?
Thus, after the Shaolin era, it was as if in the mere snap of a finger: without relying on words, silence, speech, or the categories of existence and non-existence, all was set at ease.
One loses what was gained and spontaneously returns to the source. Furthermore, those of old who dwelt in caves and lived in rock shelters did so solely because they took the Dharma to be supreme.
As for the matter of flavor, no one at all anticipated that those in between would become arrogant; only the Great Master Dazhi foresaw this.
Yet, he resolved it through the standards of the Zen forest (Chánlín). By relying on his support, the tradition of Shaolin has remained flourishing throughout the world to this day.
I wish to establish the position of Bodhidharma, the Great Wise One, within the ancestral hall of the world, with those who successively transmitted the founding lineage attending upon him.
This is to honor the arrival of later generations by respecting their origin and returning to that greatness; how could it be otherwise? The *Luohu Yalu* states:
"When Master Long resided at Tiger Hill, he traced back the story of Master Baiyun Endu’s establishment of the ancestral hall."

(And so forth). Baiyun paired Baizhang with Dharma for veneration; among those with discernment, there was none who did not approve of this proposal. It may be said that he understood the fundamental source.
The *Zengzongzan* (Hymn to the Orthodox Lineage) states: Chan Master Deshan Jianxian, whose name was Xuanjian, was the dharma heir of Longtan. Whenever the Master presided over a monastery...

He demolished the Buddha Hall, leaving only the Dharma Hall. The commentary says: This so-called demolition of the Buddha Hall—biting the pig and the dog—is the act of a venerable elder who is beyond common human sentiment;
he was surely not some master who clung to the splendor of flowered brocade or craved the itch of worldly luxury.

*The Precious Instructions* states: Suian said, "Whenever Yuetang (whose name was Daochang) served as abbot at various monasteries, he took the practice of the Way as his primary responsibility. *Yuetang Refused Offerings*: At Yuyuan, he declined numerous meals. *The Precious Instructions* says: Suian remarked, "Yuetang (name Daochang), wherever he resided as abbot, made the cultivation of the Path his own personal mission."

He did not act as a solicitor for alms, nor did he attend upon officials to seek audiences. Each year, the number of mouths to feed was met with whatever resources the monastery’s permanent endowment provided.
Many young monks who were determined to serve as guides and preachers were turned away by him. Someone asked, "The Buddha ordained that a śramaṇa should carry a bowl to sustain his life;
why does the Master refuse them and not allow it? Yuetang replied, "That would have been acceptable when our Buddha was alive. I fear that today..."
If one acts thus, there will inevitably be those who seek profit to the point of selling themselves.
Reflecting on this, I recall that the words of Master Yuetong, who spoke with profound clarity regarding the prevention of small lapses before they become grave, still ring in my ears.
Judging by today’s situation, however, it seems we have gone far beyond merely selling ourselves.
The *Yunwo Jitan* states: When Chan Master Yuquan Hao entered the kitchen and saw the evening meal being prepared, he asked, "Is this for guests arriving later, or for the assembly of monks?
When they answered truthfully, he immediately summoned the administrators and reprimanded them with his staff, saying:
"In the past, when I practiced Zen for the sake of others, I drew water and pounded rice. Now, you have ready-made rice and flour, steamed and cooked, provided as offerings."

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are no different [from you], yet you eat your fill and pay no heed to study or practice. You harbor a hundred kinds of thoughts and crave the fragrances of the five flavors;
you falsely pretend to be the intestines of a donkey, the raw flesh of a eel, the bones of a sheep, or the claws of a soft-shelled turtle. You feed eighty-four thousand families of worms;

with eyes open, you follow after sensory objects; with eyes closed, you revolve with dreams. You do not know that the Official Who Registers Salaries and the Official Who Reclaims Surpluses are watching over you.
"Indeed, by following you in recording and auditing the registers of stipends, you have taught me that the day for my own suffering is at hand.
Your followers could no longer endure such aridity and desolation, so they slandered you to the district magistrate, saying: 'The Elder cannot settle the assembly;
he does nothing but come and go, inspecting trifles. The magistrate summoned Huìhào and said to him: 'Great Good Knowledge, why are you not in your chamber?'"
He sat upright. "Have you been coming and going so much from the three gates at the two corridors?
Hao replied, "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas. Does your honor take sitting to be that Buddha? You are killing the Buddha by your sitting.
The magistrate merely smiled.

*Yung-ching San-chiao Fa-ch'uan Wan-chüan P'u-teng Lu* (The Universal Lamp Record of the Dharma Spring of Ten Thousand Volumes on the Three Teachings at Yung-ching): "Chan Master Yung-ching of Tung-shan in Fu-chou visited such renowned monks as Ta-yu Chi and Shen-ting Yin.

Later, upon meeting an elder master under the lineage of Lo-han, he finally attained thorough realization of his own nature. His reputation for the study of the Way spread far and wide, and he was highly esteemed within the monastic community."
He served as the abbot of three monasteries. Having resided at Dongshan, he moved to several other locations.
The *Fǔdēng Lù* states: "The Chan Master Fohui Faquan of Jiangshan, popularly known as 'Quán Wànjuàn' (Ten Thousand Volumes of Quán)."
The Goose Lake Water and Moon. The *Nanyue Tianze Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp by Nanyue Tianze) states:
Zen Master Dayi of Goose Lake was summoned into the inner palace by Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty for a doctrinal debate.
The Master cited the question posed by Emperor Shunzong to Śrī (Shili) Zen Master: "How can all sentient beings in this great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood? Śrī...
He said, "The Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water: it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped.

He then said to the Emperor, "If the Buddha-nature is not something to be seen, yet must be seen, how could one seize the moon in the water? The Emperor then asked, "What is this Buddha-nature? The Master replied:
This did not deviate from what Your Majesty had asked. The Emperor silently realized the True Principle and accorded him even greater reverence.

The *Lamp Records* states: The Chan Master Nanyue Huairang had a śramaṇa named Daoyi (who was later the Great Master Mazu) ask, "How should one apply the mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?
The Master said, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like planting seeds."
“Son, my teaching of the Dharma is like the rain from heaven. Because the conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way.
He asked again, “The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be seen? The Master said, “The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way.
It is the same with signless samādhi. Someone asked, “Is there arising and ceasing? The Master said, “If one regards it in terms of arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing...”
Yet that which perceives the Path is not the perception of the Path. Listen to my verse: "The ground of the mind contains all seeds;

when it meets with moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless; what is there to be destroyed, and what is there to be formed? Once he was thus enlightened, his mind transcended all bounds.
Baozhang Qiansui (The Precious Palm, Thousand Years):

The *Zhaozhou Qibai Puding Lu* states: "Venerable Baozhang was a native of Central India. In the twelfth year of the reign of Emperor Weile of the Zhou dynasty, the *dingmao* year, he descended as a spirit and received his physical form.
He held his left hand in a fist; when he reached the age of seven and underwent tonsure, it opened. For this reason, he was named Baozhang."
During the Wei and Jin periods, he traveled east to this land. He entered Shu to pay homage to Samantabhadra and remained at Daci Monastery, where he constantly abstained from food.
Each day he recited over one thousand scrolls of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras. One day he said to the assembly: "I have a vow to remain in this world for a thousand years.
This year marks six hundred and twenty-six; therefore, I am known as 'The One Who Lives for a Thousand Years'. Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Wutai and moved his residence to Zhushan.
He visited Huayan under Fazhong, Shuangfeng at Huangmei, and Donglin on Mount Lu. Eventually arriving in Jianye, he encountered Bodhidharma’s arrival in the Liang dynasty;
the Master approached him to inquire about the essential meaning and attained awakening. Not long after, he traveled to Wu, sailing downstream to the east.
From Qianqing he proceeded to Tianzhu, then went to Maofeng, climbed Taibai, and traversed Yandang. He dwelt for seventy days amidst the lush peaks of Cuifeng.
He visited two hermitages, returned to Chicheng, and stayed at Yunmen, Fahua, Zhujiri, Lipu, Chifu, Dayan, and other locations, as well as the stone grotto where the [Flying] Peak rests.
There he left the verse: "Having traveled to the ends of the four hundred prefectures of China, it is here that the wayfarer most delights to roam.
Later, he resided at Baoyan in Pujiang; all the places his master had passed through subsequently became monasteries.

On the first day of the New Year in the second year of the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, he fashioned a statue by hand. By the ninth day, the statue was completed. He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble?
Yun replied, "It is no different from you, Master. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus position.
Addressing Yun, he said, "I have remained in this world for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years. Now I am about to depart from this life. Listen to my verse:"
"Originally there is neither birth nor death; now I likewise manifest birth and death. I have attained the mind that comes and goes; having been born elsewhere, I shall return here again.
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
The *Biography of Chan Master Zhaozhou Zhenji* states: "The Master was a disciple of Nanquan. His name was Congshen. He resided at..."
The inscription on the stupa at the Prefecture states: "Did the Master attain seven hundred cycles of sixty years? The *Zuting shiyuan* says:

"Zhaozhou Congshen’s secular lifespan was one hundred and twenty years. Once someone asked the Master how old he was; the Master replied, "I have counted through a single string of prayer beads and still have not finished.
The inscription on the stupa at the Prefecture states: "Did the Master attain seven hundred cycles of sixty years? Thus, seven hundred cycles of sixty years refers to...
A general estimate was given as one hundred and twenty years, but in reality it was one hundred and sixteen years, plus eight months,
totaling forty thousand and two days.
Master Yihuai set down his burden and personally returned to attack Shi.
The *Pudeng lu* states: Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai was by trade a fisherman in his youth. As a child sitting in the stern of a boat, his father caught a fish and gave it to him to string.
The Master could not bear it and secretly threw it back into the river. His father became angry and whipped him, yet the Master remained as calm as ever.
Later, he traveled to the capital, where he received ordination at Jingde Monastery. He then departed to visit Jinluan Shan and Xianye.
There was a profound resonance with the subtle. Later, he arrived in Gusu and paid his respects to Mingjue at Cuifeng.
Upon entering the room, Mingjue said, "It cannot be so; it cannot be not so; it cannot be both so and not so. As the Master hesitated, Mingjue struck him out. This occurred several times.
He subsequently served as the water-head attendant; while drawing water and breaking his carrying pole, he suddenly attained enlightenment.

He composed a spontaneous verse, saying: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on one foot atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak, He snatches the bright pearl from beneath the chin of the black dragon.
With a single word, he exposes Vimalakīrti. Upon hearing this, Fengwen struck the desk and praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Thereafter, he sat in the seat of enlightenment seven times, and his transformative influence spread throughout the land.
The *Pudeng Lu* states: Shitou Zihui, the Abbot of Yan’an on Fisherman’s Terrace in Hezhou, was by trade a stonecutter.
He once visited Chan Master Liao of Ba’en to seek the method for settling the mind. After Liao instructed him, he abandoned his home to become a mendicant.

The Eulogy on the True Lineage says: Huishou was a stone mason by profession in his youth and was illiterate. Admiring the life of a renunciant, he sought out someone to orally transmit the *Lotus Sūtra* to him, which he then memorized and recited in silence.
He entered the service of Chan Master Jing of Nantang to perform tasks such as sweeping and sprinkling water. One day, the Master ordered him to fetch some stones.
Huishou held his hammer and struck the stone while reciting the sutras without ceasing. Huichang said to him, "Today there is a clatter; tomorrow there will be a clatter.
When birth and death arrive, how will you resolve it? Huishou was startled and set down his tools. He prostrated himself and requested the ultimate Dharma.

Consequently, he followed [Huichang] to the abbot’s quarters, where he was told to stop reciting the sutras and instead contemplate the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman. Huishou did so for a long time.
He was carving stone. The stone was hard; he exerted all his strength with a single blow of the hammer and suddenly beheld a flash of fire, at which he attained enlightenment.
He presented a verse, saying: "I have exhausted my efforts, yet there is no clue at all; the scattered sparks of light were originally right here. The Master said, "You have penetrated it.
In the preface to the *Record of Stonehead* composed by Mr. Jin-yun, it is said: "He turned back the hands that wield the hammer to strike the stone [toward the mind]."

Looking up, he struck the solid heights; his exertion being coarse and powerful, a single blow passed right through. Later, while sitting in the Mountains for Fishing, Guaiya’s rugged cliffs were ten times more formidable than those of his master.
Yian shared the toil; Zhenru personally served others.
The *Treasury of Jewels of Humans and Devas* states: "Master Quan of Yian appeared at Wannian during the Qiandao era.

When senior scholars and veteran teachers beheld his dignified demeanor and heard him expound the Dharma, they all folded their hands in reverence and were moved to spiritual intoxication. Both within and without, ten thousand fingers [of disciples] gathered like a well."
Everything was orderly, as if entering a government office. Wherever the Master traveled to practice the Way, he shared the same labors as the assembly.
Minister You Goumao remarked, "The abbot sits at ease while expounding the Dharma; why go so far as to personally engage in the ascetic practices of a *dhūta*? The Master replied, "Not so."
In the age of the Dharma’s decay, bhikṣus abound in overweening pride; having not attained [realization], they claim to have attained it, and thus seek to act according to their own whims.

I lead by example with my own person, yet I fear even this may not be followed—how much less would I dare to indulge in self-indulgence? In recent times, those who speak of the standards for the Chan forest invariably cite the Master as the foremost exemplar.
The *Sengbao zhuan* states: Chan Master Zhenru of Daopei was a man of stern simplicity and high discernment;

he took the upholding of the Dharma as his vow and disciplined himself with rigorous adherence to the Vinaya. When Shi Shizhi governed Tanzhou, he heard of Zhenru’s reputation and was delighted by it, yet could not induce him to come.
It so happened that the dharma seat at Yueyu was vacant, so he received Zhenru with the utmost courtesy and invited him to assume the position of abbot. After several days...
He subsequently took up residence there. Before long, he moved to dwell at Daowei, where his assembly numbered two thousand. There were no formal constraints; everyone disciplined themselves.

Only after the morning gruel did he receive his disciples to inquire about the Way, which was called "entering the room. After the midday meal, he would invariably assemble the great multitude for tea, visiting various quarters once or twice a month.
Yet, Zhe would lecture on the teachings without fail every day. Once the session had concluded, Zhe would personally engage in manual labor, employing others to assist him.

The official by his side was like a passerby. Morning incense and evening lamps continued for fourteen years. At night, he performed prostrations and held a bundle of *māra* grass while inspecting the lamps along the corridors of the palace halls.
When weary, he would cover his head with his *pūti* robe and doze off in the Hall of the Three Sages. He remarked:
"Truly, throughout my life, I have used my body as a tongue to speak of the affairs of the *bhikṣus*, and so forth."
*Lētán Yàogǒng* (The Mercury of Lētán) and *Yúnmén Dānshā* (The Cinnabar of Yúnmén).
The *Sēngbǎo Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) states: Master Nán of Huánglóng relied upon Master Chéng of Sānjiǎo. Chéng was renowned at the time;

upon first seeing [Nán], he recognized his potential and granted him his approval. When Chéng moved his residence to Lētán, the Master went with him. Chéng then had him share the teaching seat to receive visitors.
Wen Yue of Nanchang saw him and, every time he returned home to lie down, sighed, saying, "This man is a vessel for the Way in the South;

it is a pity he has not yet received the hammer and tongs of his true lineage. Later, they happened to travel together to the Western Hills. During a night conversation concerning the Dharma-way of Yunmen, Wen Yue said, "Although Master Cheng is a successor of Yunmen, his Dharma-way is different.
The Master asked why it was different, and Wen Yue replied: [The text continues with the dialogue regarding the differences between the lineages of Yunmen and Linji.]
Yunmen is like nine-refined cinnabar that turns iron into gold; Master Cheng’s medicinal mercury and silver are merely fit for playthings—they flow away as soon as they enter the forge.
Master Cheng grew angry and threw his pillow at him. The next day, Yue apologized for his transgression.

He further remarked: "Yunmen’s bearing was like that of a king; could he have been willing to die under such words? Master Cheng possessed the Dharma, yet he accepted a 'dead word' from another. What is this so-called 'dead word'?"
"He can truly save people! he said, and immediately turned to leave. The Official pulled him back, saying, "If that is so, who else could satisfy your mind?
Yue replied, "Shichuang Chuyuan’s skillful means surpass those of all other regions. If you wish to see him, you should not delay.
The Official pondered this silently and said, "This journey is a matter of great importance. Master Yue has taken refuge at Cuiyan, yet he sends me to see Shichuang. Having seen [him],...
What has he gained? What joy could there possibly be [in that]? On that very day, he prepared his traveling gear.
Huangbo was not much; Guizong was somewhat more so.
The *Record of Linji* states: When the Master arrived at Dayu, Dayu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Huangbo."

[The Master] came forward. Dayu asked, "What words did Huangbo have for you? The Master said, "I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times, and three times I was struck. I do not know whether I am at fault or not.
Dayu said, "Huangbo was so compassionate toward you that he exhausted himself for your sake; yet you come here to ask whether you are at fault or not. At these words, the Master—
Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment and said, "So it was; Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much at all.
Daoyu grabbed him by the collar and said, "You little bed-wetting ghost! Just now you were asking whether there was an offense or not, and now you say Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much at all.
What principle have you seen? Speak quickly, speak quickly! The Master then struck Daoyu in the ribs.
[He gave] three fists. Dayu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher Huangbo has nothing to do with me.
The *Guangdeng lu* states: "Regarding Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong Temple on Mount Lu, Huangbo said:
'Among the eighty-four spiritual friends produced by Master Mazu, when questioned, each and every one was dripping wet; only Guizong was [different]. '""'"""
A mere trifle.
The Dharma-eye is not yet realized; Great Enlightenment is too far off.
The *Lian deng lu* states: "The Chan Master Qingliang Da Fayen succeeded the Chan Master Qingliang Taiqin. Opening...
On a certain day, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "I originally intended to hide my ineptitude in the deep mountains and spend my time tending to my illness.
However, as there remains an unfinished case from my late teacher, I have come forth to bring it to a conclusion."
The *Guangdeng lu* states: Chan Master Xinghua Cunjian traveled on pilgrimage to the South. Upon his return, he served as the Head Seat (shouzuo) in the assembly of Sansheng.
He would often utter this statement: "I have traveled all over the South, yet with my staff I have never once struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma.
When Sansheng heard this, he asked him, "What kind of eye do you possess?"
He spoke thus, and the Master (Linji) gave a shout. Sansheng said, "It must be you who can do so.
Later, when the Master became the head attendant at Dajue, he continued to speak in this same manner. One day, Dajue called out, "Head Attendant!
I have heard you say that after traveling all the way south on pilgrimage, you have never once struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma. You—
"What kind of eye do you possess to speak like that? The Master then shouted. Da-jue raised his staff; as the Master hesitated, Da-jue struck him.
The next day, the Master said, "I have learned a phrase regarding guest and host from my elder brother, Master San-sheng."
"I have been completely defeated by my elder brother. Give me a Dharma-door of peace and happiness.
Jue said, "You blind fellow coming here to meet with defeat! He stripped off his patched robe and gave him a severe beating.
Under the blows of the staff, the Master realized the principle of how the late Linji had received blows from Huangbo. Later, when he ascended the hall to offer incense, he said: "This..."
"One stick of incense, originally intended for Master San-sheng, would have been too remote for me;
originally intended for Master Ta-chüeh, would have been too distant for me. It is better, therefore, to offer it to our late teacher Lin-chi."
Ye Xian’s Return of Flour; Fayun’s Tea Gathering at Wuku.
It is said that Master Xingxue of Ye Xian was stern and austere, and the *nàzi* (monks) revered him.
When Fushan Yuan and Tianyi Huai were among the assembly, they went specifically to visit and question him. It happened to be a time of snowy cold, yet Xingxue scolded and drove them away.
When the water was about to be splashed [upon him], his bedding and clothes for the night’s stay were all soaked. The other monks all departed in anger;

only Huiyuan remained, folding and stacking his sitting mat and robes, and sitting again in the guest quarters. Xingshou arrived and scolded him, saying, "If you do not leave immediately, I shall beat you.
Huiyuan stepped forward and said, "The two of us have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master. How could we—"

If one splashes it with a ladle of water, it will leave; yet even if one were to strike it to death, it would not go. Xuefeng said with a wry smile, "The two of you wish to practice Chan, so you have come to register as residents.
Subsequently, he invited Yuan to serve as the head cook (dianzuo). The community found the food austere and plain.

One day, while Xuefeng had gone out to the manor, Yuan stole the keys to take oil and flour to make a five-flavor porridge. When the porridge was ready, Xuefeng suddenly returned and went to the hall.
After the morning gruel was finished, he sat outside the hall and ordered the invitation of the *dianzuo* (head cook). Yuan arrived first and said, "I actually took oil and flour to cook the gruel;

I am willing to request that the Master punish me. The Administrator ordered that the value of the items be calculated. Once the assessment of his robes and bowl was completed and returned, Yuan was struck with thirty blows of the staff and expelled from the monastery.

Yuan stayed at a lodging in the marketplace and sought the mediation of fellow practitioners to have himself pardoned, but the Administrator would not grant permission. He spoke again, saying, "If not..."

Yonggui requested permission to join the assembly for the evening meal, but this was also not granted. One day, as he was walking through the streets, he saw Yuan standing alone in front of a guesthouse.
He said, "This is the corridor of the monastery's quarters. You have stayed here for a long time;
have you ever returned the rent? Calculate what you owe and pay it. Yuan showed no sign of distress and went to the market with his alms bowl to beg for money.

He sent him back. After another day had passed, [Dongshan] went out into the street and saw him returning with his alms bowl. Upon his return, he said to the assembly, "Yuanzhen truly has the intent to study Chan. He then summoned him back.
Wuku said: "Chan Master Mingshui Xun was serving as an attendant in the quarters of the Abbot (Fayun Si’s Yuanotong Faxiu) at Fuzhou.

At that time, Chan Master Daolin Lin had arrived for temporary lodging, and the Abbot specifically prepared tea for this new arrival. Master Xun went in person to the quarters to invite him, but Lin was not there.
A fellow practitioner sitting at the same table as Lin said to him, 'Go; wait for him to come, and I will [serve him for you].'"
"You were invited," [Yuan-tong] said. [Lin] withdrew. The assembly had inadvertently forgotten this; after the midday meal, the drum was struck to convene for tea, yet Lin did not arrive.
Yuan-tong asked, "Is the newcomer here? He sent someone to summon him. When Lin arrived, Yuan-tong ordered him to withdraw to a seat on a mat and stand before the assembly, reprimanding him:

"The mountain gate has specifically prepared this tea to manifest the formal etiquette of the monastic community. For what reason have you been so negligent as to fail to arrive at the appointed time? Lin...

He said, "Just now I heard the sound of the drum and was suddenly overcome by internal pressure; I rushed forward but could not go on. Yuancong scolded him, saying, "My drum is not *bádòu* (castor beans).
If it struck you, you would have had diarrhea. Xun came forward and said in white, "It was my failure to request [the drumming] that caused this; I shall leave the monastery.
At that time, a fellow practitioner stepped out from the assembly and said, "This is not the fault of the attendant or the newcomer; it is my own [fault]."
I had intended to submit this on his behalf, but unfortunately forgot. I should have requested the discharge for both individuals at that time.
Yuan Tong highly esteemed their integrity and magnanimity, and thus granted them both clemency.
Yangshan’s Perfect Circle. Yuanwu Keqin’s *Congrong Lu* states:
When Chan Master Yangshan Huiji first traveled to study under various masters, he visited Danyuan (whose name was Yingzhen; he was a successor of Nanyang).
Having already realized the profound essence, Danyuan said to the Master: "The National Teacher at that time received from the Sixth Patriarch the Perfect Circle."

Together they numbered ninety-seven scrolls, which were bestowed upon the old monk. He then said, "Thirty years after my passing, a śrāmaṇera shall come from the south and greatly propagate this teaching.
Transmit it in succession so that it never be interrupted. I now entrust it to you; you must uphold it.
Thereupon, he took the original texts and handed them over to the Master. The Master received them, glanced through them once, and then—
[The master] burned them. One day, Tanyuan asked, "The various images you brought previously were quite worthy of being cherished and preserved.
The Master replied, "I looked at them then and burned them right away. Tanyuan said, "In this Dharma-gate of mine, no one is able to understand it;
only my late teacher and the various patriarchs and great sages can fully comprehend it. How could you, my son, burn them? The Master said, "Huaiji."
"A single glance is sufficient to understand its meaning; however, one must apply it in practice and must not cling to the original text.
